title: The sower (Matthew 13:1–23)
hookLine: seed on the path, the rocks, the thorns, and the good ground
tomorrow: the mustard seed and the yeast

lines: A SOWER GOES OUT TO SOW.
cards: The same lake, a calmer day. So many people have come to hear Jesus that he gets into a boat, pushes out a little, and sits down to teach, while the crowd stands on the shore.

Instead of a lecture, he tells a story about farming, from the fields around that lake. In the Douay-Rheims: "Behold the sower went forth to sow." A man walks across a field, scattering seed by the handful.
Some falls on the path. Some on rocky ground. Some among thorns.
And some on good ground. That's almost the whole story.

teach.b: Today's word names this kind of story: parable. In Greek, parabolē: para, beside, and ballein, to throw. A story thrown down beside something, so you can compare them: an everyday picture laid next to the kingdom of God.
A parable doesn't explain itself. It ends, and you're left holding it. Jesus ends this one: "He that hath ears to hear, let him hear."
Now the four grounds. Seed on the path gets snatched by birds before it can sink in. Seed on rocks springs up fast in shallow soil, then withers in the sun, no roots.

teach.h: THE PATH, THE ROCKS, THE THORNS.
teach.b: Seed among thorns grows, but the thorns grow too, and choke it.
And seed on good ground bears fruit: some a hundredfold, some sixty, some thirty. Later his disciples ask what it means, and Matthew gives Jesus's explanation. The seed is the word of the kingdom.
The path is someone who hears it and doesn't understand, and it's taken away. The rocks are someone who receives it with joy, but falls away when trouble comes.
The thorns are the cares of the world and the lure of riches. The good ground hears, understands, and bears fruit. Notice the sower.
He throws seed everywhere, even on the path, even on the rocks. Seed costs something, and he's generous with it anyway. Some readers say a single person can be all four grounds, on different days.

teach.h: HE THAT HATH EARS TO HEAR, LET HIM HEAR.
teach.b: Catholics hear this parable at Sunday Mass, and some use it to examine their hearts.

how: Catholics hear the parable of the sower at Sunday Mass and some use its four kinds of ground to examine their hearts in prayer or before confession.

o: a fable where animals talk and act like people
a short everyday story that teaches about God
a true event from history retold as a lesson

games.q: what happens to the seed — tap the pairs.

s: the sower plants carefully, only on good soil
he throws seed everywhere, even on the path and the rocks.
parable comes from Greek for thrown beside
para, beside, and ballein, to throw: a story laid next to something.
Jesus tells this parable from a boat
the crowd stands on the shore, and he sits in a boat to teach.

games.q: you're the sower, with a bag of precious seed and a field with paths, rocks and thorns in it. how do you sow?
o: only on the patches you're sure are good.
you wait until the field is cleared.
games.why: the sower throws seed everywhere: on the path, the rocks, the thorns and the good ground. and the good ground yields a hundredfold.

practice: Without judging, just look at what kind of ground you are today: the path, too hurried for anything to sink in; the rocks, excited about something good but not rooted; the thorns, so full of worry and wanting there's no room; or a patch of good ground, soft and open.
There may be some of each, so find the good patch, however small, and rest there. If you pray, you can ask God to make your ground good.

wordCard.voice: Parable. From the Greek for thrown beside: an everyday story laid next to the kingdom of God. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: a comparison, literally something thrown beside. The word behind parable.

carryVoice: Your line: be good ground. Whatever the soil, the sower still scatters the seed. Day forty-three, planted.
